title: Object Storage vs File Storage vs Block Storage

blocks.text: The same photo, three ways to store it
Suppose your app saves cat.jpg. Its bytes, the numbers that represent the photo, can be stored using any of the three types.
All three can use disks underneath. The difference is what the storage system lets your application ask it to do.
Metadata means details about the data, such as size or modification time. Files have metadata too. Having metadata does not distinguish object storage from file storage.
1. Block storage: the computer receives a disk
A block volume is storage presented to a computer as a disk, even when the actual hardware is elsewhere.
The disk provides numbered locations for chunks of bytes. These are block addresses. The numbers exist before you save a file.
At this level, a write says: put these bytes at this block number. It does not say: save a file named cat.jpg.
A filesystem is software that manages filenames, folders, permissions, and where file data is stored on a disk. Your computer uses one when you save files.

Simplified example: cat.jpg is 10 KiB. KiB means 1,024 bytes. Suppose the disk and filesystem both use 4 KiB blocks. Without compression or empty gaps, the photo needs three data blocks. This excludes metadata.

Filesystem records:
  cat.jpg -> data blocks 40, 41, 90

Data in those blocks:
  40 -> first 4 KiB of the photo
  41 -> next 4 KiB
  90 -> final 2 KiB; rest unused

The filesystem chooses free blocks and remembers which ones hold cat.jpg. They need not be next to each other. The block device stores bytes at those addresses; it does not interpret filenames or photos.

App: save cat.jpg
  -> Filesystem: record name and choose data blocks
  -> Block device: write bytes at numbered locations
Choose block storage when a server needs its own disk. For example, a database can keep its data files on a filesystem you create on that disk.
2. File storage: the application receives files and folders
The app asks: open /photos/cat.jpg, read its bytes, or change bytes inside it. The filesystem handles the disk locations.
Here /photos/cat.jpg means: find the photos directory, then find the cat.jpg file inside it. A directory is a folder managed by the filesystem.
Finder and Windows Explorer show this file view. That view may come from a filesystem on your local disk or from a remote file service.
A cloud file service manages the filesystem for you. Servers connect to it and use its files through normal file operations. Amazon EFS is one example.
Choose shared file storage when several servers need the same folder, or when existing software requires file operations. Applications must still coordinate conflicting edits.
3. Object storage: the application uploads named data
The app sends the photo bytes to a service with a name. The service stores them as an object. Later, the app requests the object by that name.
In Amazon S3, a bucket is a named container for objects. A key is the full name you assign to an object inside that bucket.

Upload:
  bucket = my-photo-app
  key    = photos/cat.jpg
  data   = the photo bytes

Download:
  request bucket my-photo-app, key photos/cat.jpg
Two buckets can each contain an object named photos/cat.jpg. The bucket and key together identify which object you mean.
In an S3 general purpose bucket, photos/cat.jpg is one complete name. You do not need to create a photos directory first. This is what a flat namespace means.
S3 can list names beginning with photos/ and display them as a folder. That display does not make photos a filesystem directory.
Why this matters: a filesystem can rename a directory without copying each file. In this S3 bucket, changing photos/ to animals/ requires copying the objects to new keys and deleting the old ones.

For ordinary S3 general purpose objects, changing the photo means uploading a replacement object. Reading only a selected byte range is supported. Some object services offer additional update operations.
Choose object storage when your app mainly uploads and retrieves named data, such as photos or backups, and does not require normal filesystem editing.
